articles.title: Suspicious envelope sent to Massachusetts Elections Division
articles.text:
Suspicious envelope sent to Massachusetts Elections Division | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Federal authorities are investigating a suspicious envelope that arrived at the state's Elections Division Friday morning.
When employees in the office saw the envelope, they immediately contacted state and federal authorities, according to a statement from Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin. The U.S. Postal Service Inspection Services now has the envelope in its possession.
“I am grateful for the swift response this morning by the Massachusetts State Police, FBI, and USPIS,” Galvin said. “Because of the information we received from the FBI and USPIS before this envelope arrived, my staff was able to identify the envelope before it reached the Elections Division’s office. The Elections Division’s work was uninterrupted, and my staff remains focused on administering the upcoming election.”
Other election officials in other states, and some congressional offices, received suspicious mailings earlier this week. Some of them contained a powdery white substances, though it was not clear if that was the case for Galvin's office.

articles.title: 5 pumpkin patches around Mass. with more than just gourds
articles.text:
5 pumpkin patches around Mass. with more than just gourds | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Pumpkins for sale in a market in Carver, Massachusetts. (Getty Images)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
I’m a big fan of pumpkins and jack-o’-lanterns. (You might even say they send me out of my gourd.) They’re a seasonal decoration that’s easy enough to set up — no lights to string up or plants to water. And there’s a certain New England charm that comes with taking the time to get dressed in your autumn best to pick your own. Orange, red and yellow leaves on the ground compliment the color of the pumpkins in the patch (and, perhaps, the flannel or sweater you’re wearing, too).
If you’ve yet to pick up a pumpkin this season, this weekend is set to deliver two crisp, cool days to do so. And to help you choose where to go, we’ve pinpointed five pumpkin patches and farms in Massachusetts that offer a little extra fun for visitors.
For pumpkin picking and… plenty of eats:
Hanson’s Farm | 20 Nixon Rd., Framingham
A ticket to Hanson’s Farm this fall includes one sugar pumpkin to take home, as well as admission to its pumpkin patch and corn maze. (On Fridays and weekends, that ticket also gets you on a hayride, too.) They’ve also got several food tents serving sandwiches, s’mores and cider donuts, an ice cream bus and a beer and wine garden in addition to their farmstand. So if you’re looking to pair your pumpkin patch visit with lunch, this might be the best pick.
Cost of admission: Adult tickets are required for anyone age 13 and up and cost $20. Tickets for kids aged 6 to 12 are $15. Children under age 5 get in free.
For pumpkin-picking and… leaf-peeping:
Ioka Valley Farm | 3475 Hancock Rd., Hancock
According to the Department of Conservation and Recreation’s interactive fall foliage map, the leaves in the Berkshires are near peak this week — making for an especially scenic drive out west. So if you’d like to get a leaf-peeping road trip in while picking up a pumpkin, Ioka Valley Farm might be worth the three-hour drive from Boston. The family-owned farm Hancock offers free admission during fall weekends and includes a pumpkin patch, a petting zoo and homemade farmstand goodies like cider donuts and syrup.
Cost of admission: Visiting the farm is free. Pumpkins cost $0.80 per pound, and pumpkins over 25 pounds are capped at $20, according to the farm.
For pumpkin picking and… physical activity:
Red Apple Farm | 455 Highland Ave., Phillipston
Red Apple Farm was in the news earlier this week as the farm behind Boston’s “official pumpkin,” a giant green gourd currently on display at the Boston Public Market. The farm also has a booth at the market with cider donuts and slushies. But if you make the trip out to their growing grounds in Phillipston, you can pick from their pumpkins, potatoes, squash and corn as they harvest produce for fall. They also have hiking trails and a disc golf course — in case you’d like to get in some extra steps.
Cost of admission: The farm is free to visit. Pick-your-own pumpkins are charged at $1.75 per pound, while pre-picked pumpkins are $2 per pound.
Pumpkins at the Tougas Family Farm in Northborough. (Charles Krupa/AP)
For pumpkin picking and… photo ops:
Cityside Pumpkin Patch | 99 Autumn Lane, Boston
This Seaport pop-up is one of two Cityside Pumpkin Patches open on the East Coast. (The other is situated on a similarly trendy waterfront in Philadelphia.) The new urban pumpkin patch is taking over the Island Creek Oysters space through Nov. 1. It advertises pumpkin picking (and smashing), fall-themed mixed drinks and, of course, lots of photo opportunities. It’s received mixed reviews on social media: Some enjoyed the pumpkin patch, but others did not, citing the cost of activities and food as issues. But if you’re looking for a place to take a cute pic surrounded by pumpkins — without having to drive out to the farm — it’s a convenient option.
Cost of admission: Tickets are timed for two hours and prices vary depending on the timeslot you select, beginning at $13.90 for admission (not including a pumpkin) and reaching up to $33.25 for admission (including a pumpkin) during weekend and late-night timeslots. Click here for more information.
For pumpkin picking and… farm games:
Sauchuk’s Corn Maze & Pumpkin Patch | 200 Center St., Plympton
Sauchuk’s is a popular pick for locals — so popular, in fact, that they’re already booked out this  weekend. Admission earns you access to the pumpkin patch and a whole suite of farm games and kids’ activities. They’ve got a massive corn maze (this year’s theme is MA250), an arcade, kids’ zip line, carousel, wagon rides, and more. Just be aware: their season ends on Oct. 31 and they are only open on the weekends, so if you want to visit, you’ve got only three more days to choose from.
Cost of admission: Advance tickets are required for anyone age 3 and up. Refundable tickets are $28.95, while nonrefundable tickets are $23.95. Kids under 2 get in free.
P.S. — Sauchuk isn’t the only big local corn maze. All the Massachusetts farms included in this 2024 roundup also have corn mazes open to the public this autumn. You can check them out before the season ends around the end of October.

articles.title: Key takeaways from the final, fiery debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
articles.text:
Key takeaways from the final, fiery debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate Troy Jackson at Maine Public's Your Vote 2026 debate at the Gracie Theater in Bangor on Oct. 15, 2026. (Rebecca Conley/Maine Public)
It was likely their final face-to-face showdown in a race with potentially major national implications.
Over the hour, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson disparaged each other's records, portrayed the other as beholden to political interests far from Maine and drew laughs from the audience with their sharp barbs. At one point, Jackson even told Collins to "shut up" after she quipped that a protester obviously came from his camp.
But they occasionally agreed on issues, such as about the pernicious effects of the "dark money" that is pouring into Maine to attack and prop up both candidates.
Here are a few key takeaways from Thursday night's debate co-sponsored by Maine Public, NEWS CENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald.
Trump's shadow looms large
As he'd done throughout their three previous joint appearances, Jackson sought to portray Collins — a 30-year Senate veteran — as a key cog in a Republican majority in Congress that he says refuses to stand up to what he believes is a dangerous president.
"They will not stop Donald Trump and I do think our democracy is risk," Jackson said before accusing Trump of trying to suppress the vote in November. "Donald Trump is trying every trick in the book to keep power. And we've already seen what he will do on Jan. 6 when he led an insurrection."
And he repeated one of his favorite statistics — that Collins allegedly votes with Trump 96% of the time.
"The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there," Jackson said. "The votes that she throws away are managed votes that she already knows the outcome."
As she's done in previous debates, Collins accused Jackson of cherry-picking a number from a study that only examined about one-third of the votes that have been taken. The real figure, she said, is about 72%. And Collins pointed to years of analysis consistently showing her the most or one of the most bipartisan senators from either party.
"He is going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position no matter what," Collins said of Jackson. "We have lost a lot of the centrists and one of the reasons is we need people who will work across party lines."
The 'Oh shut up' moment
It's probably a safe assumption that both candidates have wanted to say this to the other at some point (or lots of times) during the three previous tense debates. But it took an unexpected to disruption to bring it out.
The brief scene began when an audience member began shouting at Collins about the environmental impact of data centers as she started answering a question on an entirely different topic.
"So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said, leaning slightly into the microphone.
"Oh shut up," Jackson shot back. "I did not ... I don't even know that kid."
"Oh right," Collins said sarcastically.
Just before Collins' initial remark, Jackson had been frowning and shaking his head in the direction of the protester. And from the audio and video, it seems like Jackson's "oh shut up" was more flippant than mean-spirited. The two rivals even seemed to exchange snarky smiles before the debate quickly resumed without future disruption.
Not surprisingly, the Senate Leadership Fund — one of the super PACs spending millions of dollars to support Collins — called attention to Jackson's statement in an email blast.
The protester was later identified as Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old Bowdoin College student. A press release from the Sunrise Movement — a self-described "youth movement to stop climate change and create millions of jobs in the process" — said in a press release that Elgie was part of a pattern of students confronting politicians on the campaign trail.
Some new issues and divisions
Despite this being the fourth debate, the two panelists — Maine Public chief political correspondent Steve Mistler and NEWS CENTER Maine host and political reporter Phil Hirschkorn — managed to get the candidates to weigh in on some new issues.
In some cases, they almost agreed.
Both Jackson and Collins said they were opposed to so-called "dark money," which is when political donors hide their contributions by giving to organizations that don't have to disclose their sources, such as politically active 501(c)(4) nonprofits. According to Mistler, Collins and Jackson have benefited from at least $75 million in dark money spending so far.
Collins said she has supported sweeping campaign finance reforms in the past that did not pass constitutional muster.
"I still think that there are reforms that could be made, and one of them is full disclosure of everyone who is contributing," Collins said.
"I'm 100% for overturning Citizens United," Jackson said, referring to the Supreme Court decision that opened the door to unlimited spending on campaigns and, by extension, the creation of super PACs. "I mean, billionaires have bought Congress and everyday people can't afford to buy them back."
On the issue of a guns, Collins reiterated that she would support a ban on so-called bump stocks that allow semi-automatic guns to function more like a machine gun and would support "reasonable" limits on magazine capacity. She also said would be "open" to increasing the age to purchase an assault weapon from 18 to 21.
Jackson said he opposes increasing the minimum age. But unlike Collins, he would support a ban on the purchase of assault weapons — but would not support taking them away from people who already own them.
But the rivals disagreed sharply on whether the Supreme Court should be expanded.

articles.title: What to watch for at this weekend's Head of the Charles Regatta
articles.text:
What to watch for at this weekend's Head of the Charles Regatta | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A spectator watches the 2016 Head of the Charles Regatta. (Elizabeth Gillis/WBUR)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
Gov. Maura Healey and challenger Mike Minogue clashed over abortion, energy prices, housing, ICE and more in another testy debate last night in Needham. In case you missed it, you can watch the full, 60-minute replay of the debate here — or read our recap for the highlights.
Now, let's look ahead at today:
Making a splash: The Head of the Charles Regatta gets underway this morning, rain or shine. The three-day rowing competition — the largest of its kind in the world — features nearly 12,000 rowers from clubs, colleges and schools across more than 30 countries. And according to Bracknell Baker, the vice chair of the regatta's board of directors, it will take more than a little wet and chilly (and windy) weather to cancel the event. (That's only happened twice: in 1996 because of a powerful nor'easter and in 2020 due to COVID.) "It's an outdoor sport and our competitors lean into it, and the volunteers do as well," Baker told WBUR's John Bender. "And we hope our spectators will continue to come out for all the good things regardless of, you know, wind or cold."
What to watch for Saturday: After eight races Friday morning, the action picks up Saturday. The morning features the return of an " Octogenarian 8," a team of women between the ages of 77 and 85 racing in a women's masters event. There's also a women's exhibition race that afternoon, in which every single competitor is a cancer survivor. " That's been an incredible community that has developed within rowing," Baker said.
What to watch for Sunday: The Dutch national men's eight team — which set a new world record in August — will race Sunday afternoon, along with New Zealand's gold medal-winning 2020 Olympic team and some of the top American universities. Sunday wraps up with the regatta's most sought-after event: the  parent-child double. " It is by far our most popular event," Baker said. "It sells out before any other event in the lottery."
Where to watch: You can refer to our 2023 guide on the best spots to watch rowers and tips for how to get there. (Remember: a chunk of Memorial Drive in Cambridge will be closed to drivers Saturday and Sunday.)
Learn the lingo: Coxswain? Scull? Crab? WBUR's Roberto Scalese explains all that funny-sounding rowing terminology here.
A farewell in Foxborough: The Boston Legacy play their final game in Foxborough tonight, ahead of next year's temporary move to Pawtucket, Rhode Island. The team, which was eliminated from NWSL playoff contention last month, plays Racing Louisville at Gillette Stadium at 8 p.m., before two away games to wrap up their inaugural 2026 regular season.
The big picture: WBUR's Dan Guzman reports that the team is already looking forward to 2027 — and a bit of stability — after splitting home games between different stadiums (and different types of grass and turf surfaces). Legacy President Jennifer Van Dijk said it will be an advantage for both players and fans, who can build "muscle memory" when it comes to parking, concessions and game-day routines. "All of those things matter," she said.
Eyes on 2028: Van Dijk said she's "super confident" the Legacy remain on track to open the 2028 season at their forever home: Boston's rebuilt White Stadium. The team originally hoped to play this season there, but construction was delayed amid legal challenges.
On Beacon Hill: Massachusetts lawmakers are moving to require insurers fully cover regular cancer screenings for firefighters. The state Senate passed a bill yesterday similar to one that already cleared the House in the summer. According to firefighter unions, which have lobbied for the bill, occupational cancer is the most common cause of firefighter line-of-duty deaths.
In related news:  New fire safety regulations for assisted living facilities took effect yesterday in Massachusetts, in the wake of last year's deadly Gabriel House fire in Fall River. The updated code requires annual checks on sprinkler systems and new measures for when faulty equipment is recalled. It comes after the state implemented new assisted living facility regulations in July that include requiring annual fire inspections and more frequent fire drills.
P.S.— What industry in Massachusetts does Question 8 seek to topple? Take our Boston News Quiz and see how well you know the stories we covered this week compared to other WBUR readers.

articles.title: Ayotte calls on X to suspend N.H. Libertarian Party’s account for calling for political violence
articles.text:
Ayotte calls on X to suspend N.H. Libertarian Party’s account for calling for political violence | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte on Feb. 5, 2025. (Todd Bookman photo/NHPR, File)
Gov. Kelly Ayotte wants the social media company X to suspend the account of the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire for what she says are “repeated violations” of X’s Violent Content Policy.
“This account has openly called for the assasination of elected officials from the New Hampshire Democratic Party, has said it condones murdering elected officials for their policy positions, and most recently threatened a member of House leadership,” Ayotte wrote Thursday to Michael O’Herlihy, head of Ssfety for X.
Ayotte’s letter is her most recent pushback against a longstanding pattern of caustic social media posts made on the @LPNH X account that have threatened violence against Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Executive Councilor Andru Volinsky.
The post that triggered Ayotte’s letter targeted House Democratic Leader Alexis Simpson.
“New Hampshire will be a better and freer place when @alexissimpsonnh is dead,” the post said. “(Or she could move out before that happens).”
Last Month, Ayotte called for the investigation of a separate post by the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire’s account that appeared to call for the murder of all Democratic elected officials:
“We openly support the assasination of basically every elected democrat in New Hampshire. But if you don’t have the balls to do it then you should probably vote GOP,” that post read.
The New Hampshire Attorney General’s office has declined to say whether it is investigating the media posts in question, but confirmed last month that prosecutors are aware of them.
“We would not be in a position to comment further at this time,” New Hampshire Department of Justice spokesman Michael Garrity said.
The state Libertarian Party, which is led by Manchester businessman Jeremy Kauffman, was stripped of its national affiliation in May for violating party rules.
Kauffman is a former U.S. Senate candidate, who once helped lead the Free State Project. He is close to several leading state lawmakers including House Majority Leader Jason Obsorne. At an event earlier this year, in which he announced the creation of a new "Free State Party," Kauffman said that Osborne was serving on the group's board of directors.
In an X post of his own late Wednesday, Osborne criticized the @LPNH posts: “if you were a House member and not just an anonymous account formerly affiliated with an irrelevant political party, I would insist upon your resignation,” Osborne wrote.
After Ayotte called for X to suspend the @LPNH account, Osborne added, “If I were X, I would delete that obnoxious account.”

articles.title: Aaron Sorkin's 'To Kill a Mockingbird' is beautiful and heart-wrenching
articles.text:
Aaron Sorkin's 'To Kill a Mockingbird' is beautiful and heart-wrenching | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Karen Killeen as Scout in The Huntington's "To Kill a Mockingbird." (Courtesy Liza Voll)
Beneath a tree, the limbs of which soar above the theater’s lights, a girl runs around playfully, while violist Ashley Frith provides music onstage. It’s an idyllic starting scene in The Huntington’s production of Aaron Sorkin’s “ To Kill a Mockingbird” (through Nov. 8), a heart-wrenching story that belies its beautiful beginning. The play, with its moral teachings and tragedy, is rendered in such a way that, at times, it hurts to watch.
The show is based on the late Harper Lee’s seminal Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of the same name, and the character Atticus is based on the author’s lawyer and newspaper editor father, Amasa Coleman Lee. The book centers on Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of rape and the white lawyer Atticus Finch, who seeks to save him from conviction. Sorkin’s adaptation opened on Broadway at the Shubert Theatre on Dec. 13, 2018. At first, the play was at the center of controversy, embattled in a lawsuit from Lee’s estate alleging Sorkin’s adaptation was a departure from the novel, especially concerning Atticus’ portrayal. Sorkin’s adaptation also gives a little more space for Calpurnia and Tom’s characters.
“To Kill a Mockingbird” is set in the fictional Maycomb County in Alabama, but the story it tells is an all too common one. It’s a tale where racism propels swift violence in circumstances where guilt does not need to be proven if the accuser is white, much like that of Emmett Till, who was murdered in 1955, and Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith, who were lynched in 1930 in Indiana, along with James Cameron, who survived. It’s a story where the fear of those who are othered can eclipse fairness and basic human kindness. Despite the heaviness, there’s also some levity. The writing is witty and elicits enough laughter to balance some of the brutal truths.
From left: Karl Kenzler as Atticus Finch and Rafael Jordan as Tom Robinson in The Huntington's "To Kill a Mockingbird." (Courtesy Liza Voll)
In his hometown, Atticus (a wonderful Karl Kenzler) is respected. He teaches his son Jem (a fantastic Benjamin Izaak), who has a heart for justice, and daughter Scout (a lovely Karen Killeen) to be kind to everyone no matter what they do and who they are. It’s a lesson that becomes increasingly difficult to uphold as the townsfolk point their rage toward their father for representing Tom (a passionate Rafael Jordan).
The cast is exemplary — some have starred in the Huntington’s past excellent productions “ John Proctor is the Villain,” “ The Hills of California” and “ Eureka Day.” Artistic director Loretta Greco helms the production, and she has a knack for selecting tales with big ideas that should, if we pay attention, guide us to consider other ways of thinking.
Many lines in “To Kill a Mockingbird” do just that. At one point, Atticus says, “A person is smart, but people are dumb,” pointing out how mob mentality can quickly devolve into chaos. In another line, town drunk Link Deas (a memorable Kyle Cameron), who has a short time onstage but creates a significant impact, talks of getting used to cruelty. He tells Jem and Scout that over time, they’ll build up a tolerance to it.
The cast of The Huntington's "To Kill a Mockingbird." (Courtesy Liza Voll)
“And you can't tell who's who just by looking,” he says. “Because when horror comes to supper, it comes dressed exactly like a Christian.”
It’s the line I think about the most, particularly when a masked mob intent on wreaking havoc walks menacingly through the theater aisles intent on encircling Atticus. But Scout recognizes one of the hooded men and appeals to him as the men begin their approach.
A lot of the action in the play flashes back and forth between the courtroom, where Judge Taylor presides (played by sage actor Ken Cheeseman), and the Finch house, where Jem and Scout play with a very sweet new friend, Dill (a great Andrew Stevens Purdy). Calpurnia (a terrific Patrice Jean-Baptiste) works for the Finches and has for decades. While Calpurnia’s role is a supporting one, she gets to deliver a few lines to help Atticus see the other side of the coin. Atticus’ idealism, blind belief in the law and even the people of the town is something she is trying to get him to grapple with. Atticus is an optimist, always searching for the good, and Calpurnia understands all too well that while there is goodness in the world, it exists alongside darkness.
Rafael Jordan (foreground) and the cast of The Huntington's "To Kill a Mockingbird." (Courtesy Liza Voll)
During the trial, though, it’s Mayella Ewell (a superb Jackie Scholl) whose shocking performance pushes the audience into complete silence and stillness. Scholl’s Mayella is so convincingly disturbed and frighteningly hysterical that it’s clear something is very wrong. Her accusation against Tom, who helps her with odd jobs from time to time, makes the jury and other onlookers sympathetic.
However, it’s the questions of prosecutor Horace Gilmer (a wonderful Jesse Garlick) that fail to acknowledge the supremacist system we function within that also prick the heart. Garlick’s Horace taunts Tom while asking him why he would help Mayella, especially without pay. His question implies that Tom has a choice, which he does not. If he were to refuse Mayella, another kind of judgment and violence would come his way.
But as Atticus says to Jem after he witnesses an intense exchange, “Violence and strength are not synonyms.”
Strength is just one of the attributes needed to face injustice and dismantle systems. But perhaps, as Atticus believes, it starts with teaching kids to be good and to be kind, no matter who is in front of them.
The Huntington’s production of “ To Kill a Mockingbird” runs through Nov. 8.
